newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Nest eggs, not Easter eggs, preoccupy Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Nest eggs, not Easter eggs, preoccupy Hong Kong.

text.p: Hot cross buns were on sale in Hong Kong on Good Friday but the territory seemed preoccupied with financial nest eggs rather than Easter eggs during the last big Christian festival before the return to Chinese rule.

The South China Morning Post, Hong Kong's biggest English-language newspaper, highlighted the wealthy territory's property boom rather than thoughts about Christ's crucifixion or fears that China will clamp down on religious freedoms when it takes over from Britain on July 1.

Hong Kong people also digested the news that the territory's foreign exchange reserves stood at US$63.8 billion dollars -- one of the world's biggest such stockpiles and about US$10,000 for every person in the territory.
While many of the territory's Christians, numbering about half a million out of a population of 6.3 million, filled church pews, for most people Easter was simply a time to relax.

"People do not view it (Easter) as a great holiday," said Angel Wu, retail sector analyst at MeesPierson Securities, adding that it did not compare with Chinese New Year as a time for festivities and shopping.
However the handover to Chinese rule was uppermost in the minds of the Hong Kong Alliance, a major pro-democracy group whose leading members are branded as subversives by Beijing.
The group, saying it was "spreading an Easter message of democracy and human rights", asked people to sign a petition pressing for the release of dissidents jailed in China.
The petition will be presented to Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, who has been selected by a China-appointed panel to be Hong Kong's first Chinese chief executive.
The alliance organises an annual vigil to commemorate the June, 1989, crackdown by China on student-led protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.

Many fear the vigil will not be allowed once the five- starred Chinese flag replaces the British Union Jack, despite China's assurances that Hong Kong will enjoy a large measure of autonomy when it ceases to be a British colony.
China has said that Easter will survive the transition as a public holiday, and Hong Kong will continue to have freedom of religion.
But Beijing bristled at a statement by Pope John Paul in January that the Vatican would watch closely how Catholics in Hong Kong were treated.
Telling the Vatican not to meddle, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesman said: "We would hope to have no interference in our religious affairs."

Reflecting Hong Kong's concerns that China, rather than the Vatican, will be meddling in religion, Hong Kong Catholic Bishop Joseph Zen said this month that people feared "manipulation" of the local church.

"I am afraid that there may be cases in which they (Beijing) don't understand our system and then...they will intervene without knowing that they are damaging the Hong Kong system," Zen was quoted as saying in a church publication, the Sunday Examiner.
One Hong Kong resident breaking with tradition this year was British Governor Chris Patten, who usually spends Easter in Europe.
He stayed in the territory this year, apparently because his colleagues in the British Conservative Party campaigning for the May 1 election in Britain would be too busy to see him.
